intro.heading: One wrong answer is a person. Six wrong answers is a pattern.
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care settings.
intro.paragraph: After a falls prevention session, a manager allocates a short set of questions to the day team. A week later she opens the results expecting the odd slip. Instead, six of the eight carers have chosen the same wrong answer about what to do straight after a resident is found on the floor. Nobody is careless. They all sat the same session and read the same policy. If she treats each carer separately, she will repeat the same conversation six times and the cause will stay put. Here is how that plays out.

trail.text: A trainer runs falls prevention for the day team.
Everyone joins in and the questions in the room sound confident.
The manager allocates a short knowledge check on falls to eight carers.
Six of eight chose the same wrong answer about moving a resident after a fall.
Book all six in for a retake. Nobody asks why they all went the same way.
The post fall policy is vague on when to move someone. Nobody has read it side by side with the slides.
The same wording is in the trainer's slides, so the next team will repeat the answer.
An inspector asks: “What did you change when you found the team did not understand?”

trail_close: The people were not the problem. A shared wrong answer is information about the session or the policy. Here is how CareStream helps you see it and act on it.

why.heading: A shared wrong answer is a signal about your training, not your staff
why.sub: One person missing a question is a conversation. Most of the team missing it is a different job.

cards.title: Retraining everyone hides the cause
cards.body: If the slides or the policy were unclear, another retake teaches the same unclear thing again.

cards.title: Nobody compares the answers side by side
cards.body: Each result sits in a separate record. Without a team view, a manager has to read every one to notice that six of them are the same.

cards.title: Good managers fix the wording once
cards.body: Change the slide, tighten the policy and the whole team benefits. That is faster and more likely to last than chasing six individuals.

talk.heading: The questions managers ask, and how CareStream answers them
talk.sub: Read this as a conversation. The questions are the ones we hear most.

items.q: How would I even notice that most of my team got the same thing wrong?
items.a: After you allocate the training, the Knowledge gaps view in Analytics lists the most missed questions and the weakest topics, with how many staff each one affects. A question missed by six people sits at the top, and a Monday digest email brings the same picture to you.

items.q: Is this a training needs analysis?
items.a: Not a formal one, and CareStream does not run one for you. A formal training needs analysis is something you plan and judge. What the product gives you is real evidence from the team's own answers, which is the part most managers lack when they set out to plan training around real needs.

items.q: A wrong answer goes to the carer. Do I get told?
items.a: Not each time. Nothing alerts you on every wrong answer. You see it in the Knowledge gaps view and the Monday digest, so check it each week after a new session. The carer gets an email, at most once a day and in English, and sees the question in their Follow-up tab.

items.q: So what do the carers do with a wrong answer?
items.a: They open their Follow-up tab in the Staff Hub and choose Learn & retry, a short lesson with why it matters, what to remember and a realistic situation, then a fresh question. Or they choose Just retry, the same question again. They can retry as often as they need.

items.q: What if the policy itself is the problem?
items.a: The lessons are built from your own policies where they cover the topic. Where a policy is vague or says nothing, the lesson falls back on general good practice. That difference is a clue. The free policy screening can help you find weak wording, and fixing gaps is a Professional and above feature.

items.q: Does a face to face session set this off by itself?
items.a: No. A session does not trigger anything automatically. After the session, you allocate the adhoc module yourself. On Professional and above, the face to face router can send a catch up module to the people who attended. Here is how that works.

limits.heading: It shows you the pattern. You still decide what it means.

faqs.heading: Shared wrong answers and training gaps, answered

items.q: How do I identify training needs in a care home?
items.a: Start from evidence. Ask short questions after a session, look at which ones people miss, and compare that with incidents, audits and feedback from the floor. CareStream shows the most missed questions and weakest topics across the team, which gives you a starting point to identify training needs from real answers.

items.q: What is the difference between a learning needs analysis and a training needs analysis?
items.a: In practice the two terms are used for the same job: working out what people need to learn so you can plan training. A learning needs analysis tends to focus on the person, while a training needs analysis often looks at the whole service. Either way, real answers from your team beat guesswork.

items.q: Can CareStream do a skills gap analysis for my staff?
items.a: It does not run a formal skills gap analysis. It does show where knowledge is weak, because a wrong answer to a question on a topic is recorded and grouped, so you can see weak topics and who is affected. Hands on skills still need to be observed by a competent person.

items.q: What is a training gap analysis, and is this one?
items.a: A training gap analysis compares what staff need to know with what they do know. The Knowledge gaps view gives you the second half for the topics you have checked. The first half, deciding what your team needs to know, stays with you and your policies.

items.q: What is a good way to check for understanding after a session?
items.a: Ask a few short, practical questions within days of the session, in a form people can answer on their phone. Keep them about what to do, not what to recite. Allocating adhoc training on the topic does this, and a wrong answer gives the carer a short lesson.

items.q: How do I measure training effectiveness without a big project?
items.a: Look at three things: did people answer the checks correctly, did wrong answers close after a lesson, and did practice on the floor improve. CareStream covers the first two in the Knowledge gaps view, including closed gaps in the last 30 days. For the third, use your audits and observation, and see incident led training.

items.q: Should I retrain everyone who got it wrong?
items.a: Not before you look at the pattern. If most of the team missed the same question, check the slides and the policy first. Each carer can still use Learn & retry for a short lesson, but the lasting fix is a clearer session.

guide.heading: A practical way to act on a shared wrong answer
guide.lede: When a pattern appears, resist the urge to retrain everyone. Work out the cause first.

sections.h3: Why a plain training needs analysis often starts here
paragraphs: Care providers must make sure staff receive the training and support they need, set out in regulation 18 of the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014. The same regulations expect providers to assess, monitor and improve the quality and safety of the service, in regulation 17. Looking at what the team actually understood after a session is one practical way to do both.

sections.h3: Five questions to ask before you retrain anyone
checklist: Did most of the team choose the same wrong answer, or did the wrong answers vary?
Does the trainer's wording match what your policy says on that point?
Is the question itself clear, or could a careful reader take it two ways?
Were the people who missed it in the same shift, team or training group?

paragraphs: If the slide or the policy was the cause, change it, tell the trainer and allocate the check again to the same group. If only one or two people missed it, a short conversation and the Learn & retry lesson is enough. Keep a note of what you found and what you changed. That note is useful evidence of how you learn from your own training.

guide.note: For the inspector. Keep the questions, the results, what you found and what you changed together, so you can show that you act on what your team tells you.
